paras: The Vienna, Louisiana, jail lynching took place on the night of November 6, 1882, when a group of men forced the jail at Vienna and took out four Black prisoners who had been sent there from Jackson parish for safekeeping. Two of the prisoners, charged with robbing and trying to kill an elderly white man named Ray, were found the next morning shot to death outside town, while one escaped and another was reportedly spared. An Associated Press dispatch carried the story to papers across the country, and Louisiana papers followed with their own notices.

According to the Claiborne Guardian of Homer, an old man named James Ray was attacked on a Thursday evening in October while riding to his son's place in Jackson parish. The paper said three Black men pulled him from his mule, struck him with a fence rail, cut his throat and robbed him of a small sum before leaving him for dead. Ray survived, described his attackers, and identified the men who were then arrested and lodged in the Vernon jail.
The prisoners were later moved to the jail at Vienna for safekeeping.

On the night of November 6 a body of men, described in the dispatch as 'a posse of men, supposed to be from Jackson Parish,' made the jailer open the first door and broke their way through to the prisoners. They carried out four men; one broke away at the jail door and escaped although he was fired at three or four times. Another, the dispatch said, was given 'a chance for his life' because he was thought innocent.
The remaining two were found the next morning about a mile and a half south of Vienna, dead and 'riddled with bullets.' None of the four prisoners was named in the coverage.

The Vienna dispatch said the killings created 'quite an excitement' and would 'in all probability be looked into officially.' No report of an inquest, arrest or grand jury action appears in the coverage.

Northern and Western dailies ran the Associated Press text on November 8 under headlines such as 'Murderers Lynched' in the St. Paul Daily Globe, 'Lynching Bee' in the Salt Lake Herald and 'Taken from Jail and Shot to Death' in the Sacramento Record-Union. The Memphis Daily Appeal headed it 'Taken from Jail and Hanged' and the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer 'A Double Hanging,' although both texts said the men were shot. Weekly papers reduced it to a line in roundups, under 'Judge Lynch' in Ottawa, Illinois, and 'News of the Week' in Iowa and Michigan.

Louisiana papers added local detail: the Claiborne Guardian dated the raid to the night of the 6th and said two prisoners were 'murdered,' while the Lake Charles Echo noted that the old man had recovered and recognized the prisoners. The Ouachita Telegraph of Monroe reprinted the dispatch from the New Orleans papers but said it should have stated that Ray was set upon by four Black men, robbed, beaten and his throat cut. The Donaldsonville Chief returned to the killings in a state-news summary in December.

The Charlotte Messenger described the attackers as 'a band of masked men' and said the other two prisoners escaped, details not found in the dispatch. A few rewrites put the raid on Tuesday night, but the dispatch dated November 7 says 'last night' and the Claiborne Guardian gives the 6th. Accounts of the attack on Ray also differ, with the Claiborne Guardian naming three assailants and the Ouachita Telegraph four.

reader.title: Vienna, Louisiana, jail lynching (1882)
bases: A group of men forced the Vienna jail, took four Black prisoners charged with robbery and attempted murder, and two were found shot dead outside town (A3, A4, A20).

A 'posse of men' with no stated legal authority compelled the jailer to open the jail and took out prisoners charged with robbing and trying to kill a white man, two of whom were found riddled with bullets (A3, A4); the Louisiana press called it a mob and the two 'murdered' (A20, A26).

The Associated Press dispatch from Vienna (A3, A4) is confirmed independently by the nearby Claiborne Guardian, which dated it to the night of the 6th and linked it to its own earlier report of the attack on Ray (A1, A20).

accounts.gist: A posse supposed from Jackson parish forced the jail, took four prisoners; one escaped, one was spared as thought innocent, and two were found dead riddled with bullets; they were charged with robbing and trying to murder Ray.

accounts.label: Ouachita Telegraph correction
accounts.gist: Reprinting the dispatch, the Monroe paper said it should have stated that Ray was set upon by four Black men, robbed, beaten, his throat cut and left for dead.

accounts.label: Charlotte Messenger brief

framing.detail: Most papers ran the AP dispatch nearly verbatim under headlines such as 'Murderers Lynched,' 'Lynching Bee,' 'Two Men Lynched in Louisiana' and 'Taken from Jail and Shot to Death.'
The Claiborne Guardian called the two 'murdered,' while the Ouachita Telegraph used its reprint to stress the brutality of the attack on Ray.
Weekly roundups compressed it to a line under 'Judge Lynch,' 'Crimes and Criminals' or 'News of the Week.'
